subsection: 8. The impact of World War II on independent Ireland

notes.b: The Irish government declared neutrality at the outbreak of war and called the period the Emergency. The policy rested on the state's independence and on the difficulty of defending the island.
points: The Emergency Powers Act was passed on 2 September 1939, the day after Britain and France declared war on Germany, and it gave the government wide powers over the economy and society.
De Valera's government declared Ireland neutral and refused to join the Allied side, arguing that neutrality preserved the state's sovereignty.
The Treaty ports had been returned to Irish control under the 1938 Anglo-Irish Agreement, so the state held its own coastline and ports throughout the war.
The government's reasons included the state's weak armed forces, the risk of invasion from either side, and the strong anti-British feeling among many Irish people.
The Dáil endorsed the government's neutrality policy, and most of the population supported it, though many Irish people served in the British forces.

notes.h: Censorship and the control of public life
notes.b: Neutrality was enforced through censorship of the press, broadcasting and mail, and through restrictions on public criticism of the war effort.
points: Press censorship was imposed under the Emergency Powers legislation, and newspapers were required to submit material to censors before publication.
Censorship of letters and telegrams was used to control information passing in and out of the country.
Broadcasting was restricted, and Radio Éireann was required to avoid comment that might offend the belligerents.
The Censorship of Publications Act of 1929 remained in force, and the wartime measures extended the state's power to suppress material.
Censorship was applied to films, plays and newspapers that were thought to be critical of the government's neutrality or of Britain and Germany.

notes.h: The Defence Forces, the LDF and the IRA
notes.b: The Army was expanded, and a Local Defence Force was created to supplement it. The government also interned IRA members who threatened neutrality.
points: The Defence Forces were expanded during the Emergency, and the army grew to tens of thousands of personnel by 1940.
The Local Defence Force (LDF) was formed in 1940 as a part-time volunteer force to support the army and the Garda in local defence.
The IRA was declared an illegal organisation in 1936, and the government interned its members in the Curragh and other camps during the war.
The IRA's S-Plan campaign of sabotage in Britain and in Ireland, carried out during 1939, was met with internment and tougher powers from the government.
The Army was used to guard key installations, including ports and power stations, and to maintain order on the border.

notes.b: Wartime shortages affected almost every household. The Department of Supplies, headed by Seán Lemass, controlled production and distribution, and rationing was introduced for key goods.
points: Seán Lemass was Minister for Supplies from 1939 to 1945, and his department controlled the supply and price of essential goods.
Imports fell sharply, as the war disrupted shipping and British supplies, and the economy depended on home production of food, fuel and textiles.
Fuel shortages led to a major drive to cut and burn turf, and the state's turf production was expanded through state bodies.
Rationing of tea, sugar, butter and clothing was introduced during the war, and ration books were distributed to households.
Irish Shipping Ltd was set up in 1941 to replace merchant ships lost in the war and to carry essential cargoes when shipping was scarce.
Irish seamen died in attacks on merchant ships, and the state's replacement fleet was built up in response to these losses.

notes.h: Relations with Britain, the United States and Germany
notes.b: Ireland's neutrality brought it into tense diplomatic relations with Britain and the United States, and German and British diplomats were both watched closely in Dublin.
points: In 1940 Churchill's government offered Irish unity after the war in return for Ireland joining the war on Britain's side, and de Valera refused.
British pressure over Irish neutrality and the Atlantic approaches continued through the war, even after the Treaty ports had been returned.
In 1944 the United States sent a note, known as the American Note, which asked Ireland to expel Axis diplomats; the government refused.
The Irish government did not expel the German legation from Dublin, despite Allied pressure, and kept it open until the end of the war.
On 2 May 1945, after Hitler's death was announced, de Valera visited the German legation to sign the book of condolences, a gesture that drew condemnation from Churchill.

notes.b: Dublin was bombed in May 1941, and the bombing killed civilians and drew protest from the government, which sought to keep the country neutral.
points: On 31 May 1941 German bombs fell on Dublin's North Strand, killing about twenty-eight people and damaging many houses.
The government protested to Germany over the North Strand bombing, and Germany expressed regret, though the attack was not repeated on the same scale.
Irish people also suffered from the war at sea, as Irish-registered ships and crews were attacked by submarines and aircraft.

notes.b: Many Irish people left for Britain during the war to find work, and their remittances and experience of war work affected the wider society.
points: Thousands of Irish people went to Britain for war work, in factories, construction and the armed forces, and many sent money home.
The Emergency increased the state's control over public life, and the government's authority over the press and the economy was accepted by most of the population.
Women's employment changed during the war, with many women working in the civil service and in shortage industries.
Emigration to Britain continued after the war, and the state's economy struggled with shortages in the years that followed.

notes.b: Judgements of the Emergency depend on whether one values sovereignty and survival or the costs to the economy, to civil liberties and to Ireland's relations with the Allies.
points: Achievement: the state avoided invasion and kept its sovereignty, and the government's neutrality was accepted by most of the population.
Limit: censorship, internment and rationing limited civil liberties, and the economy suffered from shortages and falling imports.
Contemporary view: the government's supporters saw neutrality as a principled defence of independence; its critics argued that it was a policy of self-interest.
Later view: historians debate the moral basis of neutrality, and the criticism of de Valera's condolence visit on Hitler's death remains a point of contention.
Neutrality and the Emergency shaped Ireland's post-war position in the Commonwealth and in the international order.

keyTerms.definition: Ireland's refusal to take sides in the Second World War, declared in September 1939 and maintained through the Emergency.
The Irish term for the Second World War period, used to describe the wartime measures that the state adopted.
The control of press, broadcasting and mail to prevent material that might offend the belligerents or challenge neutrality.
The part-time volunteer force formed in 1940 to support the Army and the Garda in local defence.
The government department headed by Seán Lemass from 1939 to 1945, which controlled the supply and price of essential goods.
The state-backed company set up in 1941 to replace merchant ships and carry essential cargoes during the war.
The 1939 Act giving the government wide powers over the economy, the press and public life for the duration of the war.
The pressure on Irish citizens to accept the state's official line on neutrality and public life, enforced through censorship and internment.
The 1944 United States diplomatic note asking Ireland to expel Axis diplomats, which the government refused.
